Electrical Safety & Standards

 Equipotential Bonding: 7 Essential Rules for Safer Plants

 A person touching a water pipe and a faulty appliance at the same time can be exposed to a dangerous voltage difference, even when the earthing looks perfect. Good bonding joins all touchable metalwork so that difference stays too small to hurt anyone.

 Earthing gives fault current a path, but it does not by itself keep nearby metal parts at the same voltage. Equipotential bonding closes that gap by joining pipes, steelwork and equipment frames with properly sized conductors.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn what equipotential bonding is, how main and supplementary bonding conductors are sized and tested, and where IEC 60364 and IS 732 demand them.


 
 
 
 What Is Equipotential Bonding?


 Equipotential bonding is the practice of connecting all exposed conductive parts and extraneous conductive parts in an installation with low resistance conductors, so that they rise and fall in voltage together during a fault. It works alongside the earthing arrangement described in TN, TT and IT earthing systems , and it is the main reason touch voltages stay safe while a protective device clears the fault.


 An exposed conductive part is the metal body of equipment, such as a motor frame, which becomes live only under fault. An extraneous conductive part is metal outside the installation that can introduce a potential, such as a water pipe, gas line or structural steel.


 
 
 
 

 Image credit: Electrical Engineering Portal . Photo courtesy of Electrical Engineering Portal, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 The photo shows an equipotential busbar, where bonding conductors from services and steelwork meet the main earthing terminal. Without it, a fault can leave a pipe at a very different voltage from the frame beside it, a classic cause of electric shock in plant rooms.

 Why Bonding Matters Even With Good Earthing


 When a phase conductor touches a metal enclosure, fault current flows through the protective conductor and develops a voltage across it. A good earth electrode, sized as shown in earthing resistance calculation , does not remove this voltage, it only sets how much current flows back to the source.


 If a nearby water pipe is still at true earth potential, a person holding both the pipe and the enclosure sees the full voltage drop on the protective conductor. Equipotential bonding pulls the pipe up to the same voltage as the frame, so the hand to hand voltage becomes small.
